title: Adaptive regret in misspecified linear bandits
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and an integer \(p\ge0\) such that, for every \(d,k,T\in\mathbb N\) with \(d,T\ge1\) and \(k\ge d^2\), and every known feature matrix \(\Phi\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\), there is one bandit policy \(\pi\) satisfying, simultaneously for every unknown mean-reward vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\max_i\mu_i-\min_i\mu_i\le1\), \[R_T(\pi,\mu)\le C[\log(2kdT)]^p\min\left\{T,\ d\sqrt T+\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)T\sqrt d,\ \frac{k}{d}\sqrt T\right\}?\] Here \(\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\|\Phi\theta-\mu\|_\infty\). The policy may depend on \(\Phi,d,k,T\), but cannot be given \(\mu\), a fitting parameter \(\theta\), the misspecification level \(\varepsilon\), or an upper bound on that level. Use the Gaussian-noise model below.
why: Features let a learner transfer information between arms, but approximation errors can make that transfer misleading. A policy that adapts to unknown error while preserving a controlled fallback would identify how much statistical benefit an imperfect model can safely provide. The requirement that one policy meet the bound at every error level is central: independently choosing a policy after learning the true error would answer a different question.
status_note: Current openness is uncertain. The precise bound is speculative in the 2020 book; checked later primary results establish important related adaptation guarantees, but this review has not verified the full displayed simultaneous bound as a theorem or excluded its coverage by existing work. This card is individually formulated and retains that status limitation explicitly.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-15; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Bandit Algorithms, Section 24.4, disproves a more optimistic adaptive regret bound and states the displayed \(\sqrt d\)-misspecification tradeoff as a speculation. Section 24.5 separately discusses dependence on action-set geometry.
Lattimore, Szepesvári and Weisz state Proposition 5.1 for finite-action misspecified bandits, including unknown approximation error. The proposition has no general small-action fallback term.

Cutkosky et al. post their stochastic-bandit combination preprint; Section 6.2 and Corollary 6 describe the exactly-linear-versus-arbitrary tradeoff. The author publication page continues to list this item as a preprint.

Hu et al. post their dynamic-regret preprint. Its checked scope is drifting reward parameters and round-specific action sets, rather than a direct resolution of the complete stationary conjectural bound.

category_assignment.reason: The question asks for sequential prediction, exploration or regret guarantees under online feedback.

importance.reason: A substantial robustness and adaptation question for a foundational sequential-learning model. The simultaneous guarantee tests whether useful linear structure can be exploited without sacrificing controlled performance when that structure is inaccurate, across arbitrary known action geometries. Its importance is broader than optimizing a bound for one fixed action set.

sentences: The question asks for one bandit policy that adapts to unknown error in a linear reward model.
It must exploit accurate features while simultaneously obeying a uniform fallback bound when those features fit poorly.
The model has finitely many indexed arms, independent Gaussian observation noise and a known feature matrix of arbitrary geometry.
The displayed tradeoff comes from an explicit speculation in Bandit Algorithms, while later papers prove closely related partial guarantees.
The formulation is now precise, but the current openness of the complete simultaneous bound remains uncertain.

definitions: There are \(k\) indexed arms, with \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\); row \(\Phi_i\) gives the known feature vector of arm \(i\). Different arms may have the same feature vector, and no full-rank assumption or bound on the entries of \(\Phi\) is imposed. The mean vector is fixed before play and does not change with time or the learner’s choices. In round \(t\in[T]\), the policy chooses \(A_t\in[k]\), then observes only \(Y_t=\mu_{A_t}+Z_t\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) are independent standard real Gaussian random variables with mean zero and variance one, independent of the learner’s randomness. A policy for fixed known \((\Phi,d,k,T)\) is a collection of Borel-measurable maps from the history \(([k]\times\mathbb R)^{t-1}\) to the probability simplex \(\Delta_k=\{q\in[0,1]^k:\sum_iq_i=1\}\), one for each round; the selected arm is sampled from that distribution using fresh private randomness. These maps do not take the unknown environment as an argument. Thus the same policy must work for all allowed \(\mu\) for that fixed known instance. Expected regret is \(R_T(\pi,\mu)=\mathbb E_{\pi,\mu}[\sum_{t=1}^T(\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i-\mu_{A_t})]\), with expectation over observation noise and policy randomness. It compares to the best fixed arm’s mean, not the largest realized noisy reward. For \(v\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The infimum in the misspecification definition ranges over all real \(\theta\), with no norm constraint. The reward-range normalization bounds regret by \(T\); it does not bound the realized Gaussian observations. Logarithms in the displayed guarantee are natural. The single exponent \(p\) and multiplicative constant \(C\) are chosen before all instance parameters, so all hidden logarithmic losses are uniform powers of \(\log(2kdT)\). This is an information-theoretic policy-existence question: the number of reward observations is the resource, and no running-time, finite-precision representation or efficient implementation requirement is imposed on the measurable policies.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this policy-existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must provide the policy family and prove the simultaneous expected-regret bound with one universal \(C,p\), over the entire stated domain and without access to the misspecification level. A negative answer must rule out every universal pair \(C,p\), with an instance on which every policy has some admissible mean vector violating the bound; the violating mean vector may depend on the policy but is fixed before play. A guarantee only at zero misspecification, only for a known misspecification bound, or without the second uniform fallback term does not meet the target. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this asymptotic existence question.

context_blocks.text: The draft grouped two directions from the book. Section 24.4 makes the concrete conjectural claim with the minimum of \(d\sqrt T+\varepsilon T\sqrt d\) and \((k/d)\sqrt T\) when \(k\ge d^2\). This explicit simultaneous-adaptation statement is the card’s main target. Section 24.5 also asks more broadly for action-set-dependent regret characterizations; that broader direction is retained as context rather than silently folded into a second answer criterion.

The mathematical conventions are fixed against the chapter’s Gaussian model and the companion paper’s unit reward-range normalization. Indexed arms allow repeated feature rows, as in the book’s own lower-bound example. The additional T term records the trivial regret ceiling, and the explicit logarithmic factor spells out the book’s soft-O convention. These choices are recorded rather than left to the solver.

Lattimore, Szepesvári and Weisz’s Proposition 5.1 gives a finite-action guarantee of order \(\sqrt{dT\log(Tk)}+\varepsilon T\sqrt d\log T\) without requiring the error level as an input. This supports the first component of the desired tradeoff, but that theorem does not state the simultaneous \((k/d)\sqrt T\) fallback for all mean vectors.

Cutkosky, Das and Purohit’s Section 6.2 proves a frontier for performance on exactly linear rewards versus arbitrary rewards. Its Corollary 6 distinguishes these two cases. The present displayed bound also tracks every intermediate misspecification level; the two-case theorem alone is not recorded as a proof of that complete bound.

Hu, Yao, Zhang and Zhou’s July 2026 preprint uses misspecification-dependent guarantees for nonstationary bandits with changing feasible actions. Its principal claims concern dynamic regret and the variation of a time-dependent reward parameter. The checked statements do not directly assert the finite-action stationary bound on this card.

Current openness remains uncertain. The original book labels the displayed tradeoff speculative, and later work proves closely related adaptation results. This review recovers the exact target and checks several relevant theorem statements; it does not establish that no existing combination or later theorem already gives the complete guarantee.
